terms.definition: Clinical score used to estimate hemorrhagic versus ischemic stroke probability when CT is unavailable; uses consciousness, vomiting, headache, diastolic blood pressure, atheroma markers, and atrial fibrillation.
Anxiety disorder with recurrent unexpected panic attacks and ongoing concern or behavioral change related to attacks, commonly with palpitations, dyspnea, sweating, and fear of dying.
Midbrain alternating syndrome with ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral pyramidal weakness.
Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness, cognition, often due to medical, toxic, metabolic, or neurologic causes.
Scale assessing eye, verbal, and motor responses; motor M4 is withdrawal from pain, M5 localizes pain, M6 obeys commands.
Peripheral vestibular disorder characterized by episodic vertigo, hearing symptoms, tinnitus, and aural fullness.
Psychotic symptoms judged secondary to an organic brain or medical condition; must be separated from delirium when consciousness is impaired.
Personality pattern with rigidity, perfectionism, excessive orderliness, and control.
Vertigo caused by central nervous system pathology; nystagmus may lack latency and is less position-fatigable than peripheral vertigo.
Acquired decline in cognition that interferes with daily function, often involving memory, language, praxis, recognition, and executive ability.
Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation, such as enclosed spaces in claustrophobia.
Tension-type headache occurring on 15 or more days per month for more than 3 months.
Rapid flow of speech/thoughts with shifting associations, classically a disorder of thought stream/form.
Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder causing fatigable weakness, commonly ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar symptoms.
Tuberculous infection of meninges; CSF often shows mononuclear pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein.
Migraine subtype with reversible focal neurologic symptoms, commonly visual aura, preceding or accompanying headache.
Procedure to obtain cerebrospinal fluid for analysis, central in meningitis diagnosis when not contraindicated.
Head injury severity category typically associated with GCS 9-12 and intermediate loss-of-consciousness/PTA criteria.
Cognitive decline due to cerebrovascular disease, often stepwise and associated with focal neurologic history.
Steno-occlusive intracranial vasculopathy with collateral vessels giving a puff-of-smoke angiographic appearance.
Drugs used for psychosis; typical agents mainly antagonize dopamine D2 receptors, while atypical agents also affect serotonin and other receptor systems.
Acute neurologic deficit due to cerebral ischemia or infarction.
Ascending sensory tract carrying pain and temperature information.
Antidepressant class that inhibits SERT and reduces presynaptic serotonin reuptake.
Inability to form new memories after an event or brain insult.
Usually slow-growing extra-axial non-glial tumor arising from meningothelial arachnoid cap cells.
Progressive neurodegenerative dementia usually beginning with episodic memory impairment.
Motor pathways descending from cerebral cortex/brainstem to spinal motor neurons, including corticospinal tract.
Episodic flaccid weakness related to muscle ion-channel dysfunction, often triggered by carbohydrate load or potassium shifts.
Bleeding into subarachnoid space, classically causing thunderclap headache, neck stiffness, and possible subhyaloid hemorrhage.
Maladaptive pattern of substance use with impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacologic criteria such as tolerance/withdrawal.
Failure to recognize objects, persons, sounds, shapes, or smells despite intact primary sensory function.
Clinical or historical factors that increase stroke probability, including hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, hypercoagulability, and vascular disease.
Theory linking depression to dysregulation of monoamine neurotransmitters such as serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine.
Transient focal neurologic dysfunction due to ischemia without established infarction.
Neurologic deficit caused by intracranial bleeding, often associated with severe headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness, and hypertension.
Neuropsychiatric syndrome due to thiamine deficiency, with Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff amnesia spectrum.
Motor adverse effects of dopamine blockade including acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and dyskinesia.
Diffuse brain dysfunction, usually presenting with altered mental status.
Deep nuclei including caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus involved in extrapyramidal movement modulation.
Generalized seizure type with brief staring spells and classically 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG.
Preoccupation with having or acquiring serious illness despite reassurance, with absent or mild somatic symptoms.
Substances that alter perception, thought, and affect, potentially causing hallucination-like experiences.
Extra-axial hemorrhage between skull and dura, classically biconvex/lens-shaped and associated with lucid interval after trauma.
Bleeding between dura and arachnoid, commonly due to bridging vein rupture and crescent-shaped on CT.
Bleeding within brain parenchyma, commonly associated with chronic hypertension.
Cerebral lobe involved in executive function, behavior regulation, motor planning, and language production.
Major descending voluntary motor tract; lesions cause upper motor neuron weakness.
Older DSM multiaxial format separated clinical disorders, personality/intellectual disorders, medical conditions, psychosocial factors, and global functioning.
Posterior fossa tumor that may cause headache, vomiting, vertigo, ataxia, dysmetria, and dysarthria.
Functional neurologic symptoms not explained by known neurologic disease and associated with psychological mechanisms.
Brainstem reticular system essential for arousal and consciousness, working with bilateral cerebral hemispheres.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used symptomatically in Alzheimer dementia.
Recording of brain electrical activity used to support epilepsy diagnosis.
Narcotic group recognized for medical/scientific use under Indonesian narcotic classification, including agents such as pethidine.
Personality pattern marked by suspiciousness, mistrust, grudges, and hostile interpretation of neutral events.
Acute peripheral facial nerve palsy, commonly treated early with corticosteroids.
Fixed false belief not corrected by evidence and representing a disorder of thought content.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure with tonic stiffening, clonic movements, impaired consciousness, and postictal state.
Drug class acting on opioid receptors; used for strong analgesia and commonly causing constipation.
Brainstem syndrome involving lower cranial nerve and long-tract signs, such as dysphagia, dysarthria, sensory deficits, and reflex abnormalities.
Acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending weakness, areflexia, and possible respiratory compromise.
Cholinesterase inhibitor used for Alzheimer and related dementias.
Generalized febrile seizure lasting under 15 minutes, occurring once in 24 hours, without focal features in a neurologically normal child.
Typical antipsychotic used for psychosis and severe agitation, including selected delirium cases under clinical monitoring.
Straight-leg-raise test used to assess lumbosacral radiculopathy/sciatic nerve irritation.
